content:
In my attempts to turn docs#Set into a structure, the defeq abuse of Set X = X -> Prop with docs#Filter.EventuallyEq or docs#Filter.EventuallyConst is the main roadblock. I see 3 ways to resolve this.

  • introduce new definitions (e.g., EventuallyEqSet and EventuallySubset, better names are welcome)
  • migrate to something like (· ∈ s) =ᶠ[l] (· ∈ t), possibly with a specialized notation;
  • like :up: but introduce a CoeFun instance for Set turning s x into x ∈ s

Pros and cons as I see them

  • with new definitions, we have to duplicate a bunch of lemmas (or write a metaprogram that "specializes" a lemma to Sets)
  • with (· ∈ s) =ᶠ[l] (· ∈ t), Lean will simplify x ∈ s, so we can't have lemmas about, e.g., images, preimages, unions etc without reformulating them in terms of predicates.
what are some of the defeq abuses that need fixing?
A common pattern is to use s =ᶠ[𝓝 x] t or s =ᵐ[μ] t
See also #mathlib4 > local equality of sets and #mathlib4 > (simp) normal forms for expressions about `Filter`s

My engineering mind tells me (· ∈ s) is the safe option here given this is related to the backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency change and it sounds like we'd like to fix it in one go with minimal breakage. Specialized notation sounds cool but probably something for the next major version
The version that doesn't require changing simp-normal forms is "add new definitions".
Oh hmm, yeah I overlooked the simp problem
If we're going forward with new definition (that's what I have in my local branch), then suggestions for a better name for EventuallyEqSet are welcome.
I think it’s time to finally stop writing that awful s =ᶠ[𝓝 x] t and switch to 𝓝[s] x = 𝓝[t] x.
It is infinitely more readable anyway.
What do you suggest for the ae filter?
And use F ⊓ 𝓟 s = F ⊓ 𝓟 t for the other filters when needed.
If it happens very often with ae then we can have a dedicated notation like we have for 𝓝[s] x
You weren't so critical to s =ᶠ[𝓝 x] t (and the ae version) in #mathlib4 > (simp) normal forms for expressions about `Filter`s

Notes:

  • I may be biased, because AFAIR I've started using this notation (first for measure theory, then for nhds)
  • I think that consistency is more important than which of these forms we choose
  • I'm sorry we haven't asked @Patrick Massot for more details about the thumbs down reaction before going forward in #mathlib4 > local equality of sets
  • see previous 2 threads for context. Let me tag @Sébastien Gouëzel , @Anatole Dedecker , @Yaël Dillies , @Eric Wieser , @Vincent Beffara, and @Jireh Loreaux who participated in the previous 2 threads on this topic.
For s =ᶠ[𝓝 x] t, I think we can just use 𝓝[s] x = 𝓝[t] x which is mathematically equivalent. For s =ᵐ[μ] t, I'd say introduce a new definition. Are there uses for other filters?
I also saw this used for docs#residual in docs#closure_residualEq
So, I think that the new definition should be about a Filter, not a Measure.

I think that we should wait for more opinions this time before making the decision. Last time, we moved to s =ᶠ[𝓝 x] t based on a few comments, so we're reconsidering the choice just 17 months later.
While we're at it, what would be a good name for docs#Filter.EventuallyConst specialized to sets? It says that the set is null or a.e. all (in the case of the ae filter).
One technical reason to prefer the s =ᶠ[𝓝 x] t spelling is that we can have @[gcongr] lemmas for union etc.

Another alternative spelling: bihimp s t ∈ 𝓝 x
(bihimp is the complement of the symmetric difference)
While the name is strange, I think it's easier to understand than equality of filters.
We could also add notation for bihimp.
(edit: apparently open scoped symmDiff gives s ⇔ t)

import Mathlib

variable {X : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] {x : X} {s t : Set X}
open Topology Filter

theorem foo : s =ᶠ[𝓝 x] t ↔ bihimp s t ∈ 𝓝 x := by
  suffices bihimp s t = {y | s y = t y} by rw [EventuallyEq, Filter.Eventually, this]
  ext y
  change _ ↔ (y ∈ s) = (y ∈ t)
  rw [← compl_symmDiff]
  grind

What about this idea ((b) below) of Yury's from the other thread? It seems not so problematic to me if we make Set into a 1-field structure. (this is for dealing with the s =ᶠ[l] t issue)
Yury G. Kudryashov said:

Possible solutions to the defeq abuse are (a) add a set-specific notation that unfolds to (· ∈ s) =ᶠ[𝓝 x] (· ∈ t); (b) turn Set _ into a one-field structure with coercion to function given by (· ∈ s).

:face_palm: I just realized that in my reading I failed to notice that this suggestion is in the OP for this thread.
Overall though I think I agree with Patrick Massot that we should consider this an equality of filters, not an eventual equality of sets. I too find the latter a bit confusing.

For the purpose of measure theory I think stating it as "s and t coincide almost everywhere" matches mathematical practice the best. It is even quite common in some areas of maths to quotient out the sets by this relation, exactly as we do for functions.
Viewing it as an equality of filter works well if people have in mind the vision as generalized sets, but my main issue is that it is often less practical to work with, because you can't use our wonderful Eventually API. If you are working up to measure zero all the time, it is much more convenient to put your almost equality of sets inside a filter_upwards (or a docs#Eventually.mono) together with everything else that holds almost everywhere, while putting an equality of filter into the mix will end up quite painful I believe.
Note also that we use docs#Filter.EventuallyLE for eventual inclusions of sets, see docs#MeasureTheory.measure_mono_ae
(I guess another possibility would be to make filter_upwards more powerful ?)

Anatole Dedecker said:

it is much more convenient to put your almost equality of sets inside a filter_upwards (or a docs#Eventually.mono) together with everything else that holds almost everywhere, while putting an equality of filter into the mix will end up quite painful I believe.

Can we just have the lemma which converts the equality of sets into the eventual iff statement for set membership, so it's (relatively) easy to filter_upwards?

If we end up making a new definition and can make this using dot notation then this is perfect. I would be a bit sad if we can't make it through dot notation, but as long as it's a single lemma that would be okay.
I agree the interaction with filter_upwards/Eventually.mono is important to keep in mind.

Currently, I have a branch that introduces new definitions EventuallyEqSet/EventuallySubset, copies parts of the API, introduces notation for the new relations, and migrates Mathlib to it. I did it for migrating Set to a one-field structure, so it's mixed with other changes at the moment. The branch doesn't change EventuallyConst yet (just uses it on fun x => x \in s). I find dot notation and @[gcongr] lemmas for the new relations very useful. It would be nice if someone tries to migrate a few files to the "equality of filters" approach to see how it goes, then shares the experience here.

@Yaël Dillies Can you comment on how the PR was created? Is this a search-replace? Or are there cases where the replacement shouldn't/didn't happen?
From the PR description: "Generated by Claude Opus, reviewed line by line by myself."
There should be no case of missing change (except for master diverging ofc) because these changes were extracted from #41506 which I got to build locally once

Did mr Claude Opus use a sed script to generate the change?
I certainly would prefer a sed script. The are concise, deterministic, and easy to reason about.
Bonus points if 1 commit creates the new notation, and the other contains the result of running the sed script.
We have automation to verify that a commit was actually generated by running a script: that's even easier to verify.
Unfortunately that automation is slightly broken. But it's in the process of being fixed.

Johan Commelin said:

Did mr Claude Opus use a sed script to generate the change?

I understand the concern, but how could it? The information of whether the two sides of a relation are of a certain type is impossible to obtain reliably without running Lean itself, and the latter is precisely what I have done: By fixing CI on #41506, I was forced to disambiguate between the uses of EventuallyEq on functions vs on sets. The relevant changes were then extracted to #41533.
Aha, then I misunderstood. Not all instances of the original pattern have been replaced by the new pattern.
